overview:
Kayotsarga (Sanskrit: कायोत्सर्ग, Prakrit: काउस्सग्ग Kāussagga) is a central Jain meditative and ascetic posture whose literal meaning is “abandonment of the body” (kāya = body, utsarga/ossagga = giving up, renunciation). In doctrinal terms it signifies the deliberate withdrawal of attention from the physical body and its comforts, and the cultivation of awareness of the soul (jīva) as distinct from the body. It is both a physical posture and a mental discipline: the practitioner remains motionless—most characteristically in a standing position—with the arms relaxed alongside the body, feet slightly apart, and the gaze steady, while internally focusing on equanimity, repentance, and detachment.

Within Jain practice, kayotsarga is counted among the six essential duties (āvaśyaka) of ascetics and is also prescribed for lay followers, especially in the context of pratikramaṇa (ritual confession and repentance) and sāmāyika (equanimity meditation). The posture is closely associated with the ideal of non‑attachment (asaṅgatā) to the body and with the purification of karmic impurities that obscure right knowledge (jñāna), right perception (darśana), and right conduct (cāritra). Classical sources describe kayotsarga as a means of “healing the wounds” of the soul caused by passions and wrong belief, and as a technique for cutting off harmful karmas through repentance, purification, and the removal of inner “thorns” such as deceit and craving.

Iconographically, kayotsarga is one of the two principal postures in which Jinas (Tīrthaṅkaras) are depicted—the other being the seated meditation posture. Many Tīrthaṅkaras are said to have attained liberation (mokṣa) while standing in kayotsarga, and the famous colossal image of Bahubali (Gommateśvara) at Śravaṇabeḷgoḷa is a paradigmatic representation of unflinching standing meditation in this posture. The stillness of the body, even to the point of vines growing around the legs in Bahubali’s legend, symbolizes complete inner steadfastness and detachment.

Ritually, kayotsarga appears in the Āvaśyaka tradition as a structured practice accompanied by specific Prakrit formulas. It is performed after confession (ālocanā) and pratikramaṇa, and before or within other meditative acts. The practitioner declares the intention to stand in kayotsarga for the sake of atonement (prāyaścitta), purification (viśuddhi/visodhikaraṇa), removal of inner “arrows” (viśalya/visallīkaraṇa), and the destruction of sinful karmas. In later systematic works such as Hemacandra’s Yogaśāstra, kayotsarga is explained as a disciplined abandonment of bodily motion undertaken to cut off karmic bondage, supported by repentance and inner purification.

In contemporary Jain contexts, kayotsarga continues to be practiced by both Digambara and Śvetāmbara communities, though details of posture, duration, and associated liturgy may vary by sect and lineage. Modern meditation movements such as prekṣā‑dhyāna have reinterpreted kayotsarga as a form of “relaxation with awareness,” emphasizing its psychological benefits while retaining its traditional roots in ascetic discipline. Across these variations, the core meaning remains: kayotsarga is the intentional, ethical, and contemplative renunciation of bodily attachment in order to realize the true nature of the self and progress toward liberation.

primary_sources.title: Āvaśyaka-sūtra (Kayotsarga formula)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to early Jain canonical redactors; exact authorship uncertain
primary_sources.original_text: तस्स उत्तरीकरणेणं पायच्चित्तकरणेणं विसोधीकरणेणं विसल्लीकरणेणं पावाणं निग्घायणट्ठाए ठामि काउस्सग्गं तावकारियं ठाणेण मोणेण झाणेण अप्पाणं वोसिरामि
primary_sources.transliteration: tassa uttarīkaraṇeṇaṃ pāyaccittakaraṇeṇaṃ visodhīkaraṇeṇaṃ visallīkaraṇeṇaṃ pāvāṇaṃ nigghāyaṇaṭṭhāe ṭhāmi kāussaggaṃ, tāvakāriyaṃ ṭhāṇeṇa moṇeṇa jhāṇeṇa appāṇaṃ vosirāmi
primary_sources.translation: “For the sake of further excellence, for the performance of atonement, for purification, for the removal of ‘arrows’, for the destruction of sinful karmas, I perform kayotsarga. By standing, by silence, by meditation, I elevate my own self.”
primary_sources.notes: This formula occurs in the Āvaśyaka tradition as the declarative statement made by the practitioner when entering kayotsarga. Hemacandra, in his Yogaśāstra auto‑commentary, explains that ṭhāmi (“I stand”) here means “I perform” kayotsarga, understood as the abandonment of bodily motion for the purpose of cutting off karmic bondage. The terms pāyaccitta (prāyaścitta), visodhīkaraṇa (purification), and visallīkaraṇa (removal of inner ‘thorns’) describe successive aspects of repentance and inner cleansing that support the practice.

primary_sources.title: Ācārāṅga-sūtra
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Mahāvīra’s disciples; canonical Śvetāmbara text
primary_sources.translation: “(He is) an ascetic who has given up the body.”
primary_sources.notes: Although the term kayotsarga itself does not appear in the Ācārāṅga-sūtra, the expression “kayaṃ vosajjamaṅgāre” (“one who has given up the body”) is used to characterize the ideal ascetic. Later tradition connects this notion of ‘giving up the body’ with the formalized practice of kayotsarga, interpreting it as the abandonment of attachment to the body rather than physical self‑harm. The emphasis is on inner detachment and steadfastness in meditation.

primary_sources.title: Sūtrakṛtāṅga-sūtra
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to early Jain canonical redactors; canonical Śvetāmbara text
primary_sources.translation: “One who has abandoned the body is called an ascetic.”
primary_sources.notes: This passage reinforces the ideal of bodily abandonment as a defining trait of the true ascetic. Later commentators and modern scholarship see this as an antecedent to the more technical notion of kayotsarga. The abandonment is doctrinally understood as non‑attachment to the body and its movements, not as neglect of health or self‑destruction.

primary_sources.title: Yogaśāstra (Hemacandra’s auto-commentary on kayotsarga)
primary_sources.author: Hemacandra (12th‑century Jain monk and scholar)
primary_sources.original_text: तस्स उत्तरीकरणेणं पायच्चित्तकरणेणं विसोधीकरणेणं विसल्लीकरणेणं पावाणं निग्घायणट्ठाए ठामि काउस्सग्गं //
primary_sources.transliteration: tassa uttarīkaraṇeṇaṃ pāyaccittakaraṇeṇaṃ visodhīkaraṇeṇaṃ visallīkaraṇeṇaṃ pāvāṇaṃ nigghāyaṇaṭṭhāe ṭhāmi kāussaggaṃ
primary_sources.translation: “For the sake of further excellence, for the performance of atonement, for purification, for the removal of ‘arrows’, for the destruction of sinful karmas, I perform kayotsarga.”
primary_sources.notes: Hemacandra cites this Āvaśyaka formula and explains kayotsarga as the abandonment of bodily motion undertaken to cut off karmic matters such as knowledge‑obscuring karma. He clarifies that ṭhāmi (‘I stand’) should be understood as ‘I perform’, and that kayotsarga is supported by prāyaścitta (partial atonement), viśuddhi (complete purification), and viśalya (removal of inner ‘arrows’). His treatment is a key medieval exposition of how and why Jains practice kayotsarga, especially in temple ritual and lay discipline.

misconceptions.myth: Kayotsarga is simply a physical standing posture used for idol worship or ritual display.
misconceptions.reality: While kayotsarga is visually expressed as a standing posture, its primary meaning is contemplative and ethical. The posture is a vehicle for withdrawing attention from the body, cultivating equanimity, repentance, and detachment, and purifying karmic impurities. Iconic images of Jinas and Bahubali in kayotsarga symbolize inner steadfastness and non‑attachment, not mere ritual formality.

misconceptions.myth: Kayotsarga involves harming or neglecting the body and is a kind of self‑mortification.
misconceptions.reality: Classical Jain sources describe kayotsarga as ‘abandonment of the body’ in the sense of renouncing attachment and unnecessary movement, not in the sense of self‑harm. The practice is framed within strict non‑violence (ahiṃsā) and is supported by repentance, purification, and ethical restraint. It is not a license to ignore health or engage in dangerous austerities, and questions about extreme fasting or bodily harm require guidance from qualified teachers and medical professionals.

misconceptions.myth: Kayotsarga is only for monks and has no relevance for lay followers.
misconceptions.reality: Although kayotsarga is one of the six essentials of ascetics, it is also integrated into lay ritual, especially pratikramaṇa and sāmāyika. Lay practitioners perform shorter, guided forms of kayotsarga to cultivate equanimity, confess and repent misdeeds, and strengthen non‑attachment. The intensity and duration differ from monastic practice, but the underlying principles apply to both.

misconceptions.myth: All Jain sects practice kayotsarga in exactly the same way.
misconceptions.reality: The core idea of kayotsarga—abandonment of bodily attachment and motion for contemplative focus—is shared across Jain traditions, but details of posture, liturgy, and emphasis vary by sect and lineage. Digambara and Śvetāmbara communities, as well as sub‑traditions like Sthānakavāsī and Terāpanth, may differ in how they integrate kayotsarga into daily rites and meditation systems. These variations reflect historical development rather than disagreement about the basic meaning of the practice.
